speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, is the approach taken in these 12 cases different from the approach taken in the well-known case issued in September 2015, when the prosecution actually appealed on the basis that a sentence was manifestly excessive?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The reason for the prosecution doing so is explained as that it is a stakeholder in the criminal justice system and it must also do its part to ensure a fair and proportionate sentence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, may I ask whether the Home Detention Scheme and the Remission Scheme would be afforded to the persons involved in this Court of Appeal decision as well as the 12 cases that the hon Minister mentioned?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If so, would the Court of Appeal decision be a factor for the Executive to consider in making an appropriate determination in these schemes?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The first question is, by reference, to Airocean.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Airocean case dealt with an acquittal issue.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I have here an article from Channel NewsAsia published on the —

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You are referring to the case where the Public Prosecutor appealed?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By reference to that case or by reference to the Airocean case, whichever, the position here is slightly different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Professional agents or agents form only one category.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They were convicted qua public servants; they hold very different positions, senior to junior.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is no intention of doing anything about them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One is an attorney and another eight are agents of various kinds, like insurance agents, real estate agents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you can see that the principles applied in the context of Airocean for revision as well as for appeal in the other case, do not apply.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I may go further, we have talked about 16 cases, at least, where directors, qua directors, have been convicted in the past 40 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There have been more than that; but 16 reported cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What would hypothetically be the position if one or more of them would be serving sentences now?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think that can be looked at; you can argue it either way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if you look at, for example, the last case on revision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was a conviction under the Securities and Futures Act (SFA).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At trial, eventually, they were held to be not guilty because the fact that was said to not have been put out was held by the Court to be not material.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you can imagine, therefore, on the very same facts, the earlier conviction, in all fairness, ought not to stand.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Here, if any persons are serving as directors, they would have been convicted properly on the facts and on the law as had been applied by the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whether subsequently a change in law should, therefore, apply to anyone who is currently serving, or any of the several cases which have been dealt with over 40 years, there is, as Mr Pillai would appreciate, a lot of learning on that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member's second question was on Home Detention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is the Member asking by reference to these 12 cases or the City Harvest cases?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the 12, I will need to go and check.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think some may already be serving under Home Detention because there are some principles which are laid out under the rules.
